props.title: Torso
props.initialSlug: Masked killer stalks female students in Italy

sections.content: Torso (1973) stands as one of giallo's most influential entries, with director Sergio Martino crafting a template that would shape slasher films for decades. The film's stalking sequences through Perugia's medieval streets directly influenced later works like Halloween (1978) and Friday the 13th (1980). Martino's use of the killer's POV shots and methodical building of tension became standard elements of the genre. The film's explicit mix of sexuality and violence epitomized Italian thriller conventions while pushing boundaries that mainstream American horror would later embrace.

sections.content: Martino's direction in Torso showcases giallo's signature elements at their peak - the black-gloved killer, elaborate murder sequences, and red herrings that keep viewers guessing. The film's infamous scarf murders influenced Dressed to Kill (1980) and Tenebre (1982). The extended climax, where Suzy Kendall's character hides in silence while the killer disposes of bodies, creates unbearable suspense that later slashers would frequently emulate.

The film's exploration of voyeurism and sexual politics reflects themes that would become central to the slasher genre. Like Peeping Tom (1960) and Black Christmas (1974), Torso examines male gaze and sexual violence in ways that prefigured academic analysis of horror cinema. The killer's fetishistic focus on the scarf mirrors similar objects of obsession in films like Opera (1987) and The New York Ripper (1982). SUBHEAD: Impact on American Slashers

sections.content: Torso's influence on American horror can't be overstated. The film's structure - establishing multiple potential victims before isolating the final girl - became a slasher standard. John Carpenter acknowledged Torso's impact on Halloween (1978), particularly in how both films use architecture and space to create tension. The university setting and focus on young female victims would become genre staples in everything from Black Christmas (1974) to Scream (1996).
